chapter: Rasch's notes on Whiting and Berlin
title: Rasch on the Whiting and Berlin story and her trips to New York
summary: Rasch explains the New York recordings and repeats Johnson's story that Whiting and Berlin wrote a song and Berlin heard 'Believe It, Beloved'.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them
story.community_name: Working with Sinatra: bands, Vegas and the Sands

blocks.x: The preceeding taping had been done in New York City where I would travel to visit JC. He moved into the Margo Residence after leaving the hospital; as much as he wanted to come back to Wortsboro, he knew that New York City winters were much less severe than winters in Sullivan County ... and he was so right.
Now a side note on George Whiting and Irving Berlin, whom JC held in such great regard. JC told me this little story which, unfortunately, is not on the tape, but it's a
good story, and I'm repeating it here.
These are the words of JC:

George Whiting, who was a partner of mine, was one of the few names who collaborated with Irving Berlin. They wrote "When My Wife's Going to the County, Hooray, Hooray" -- George Whiting thought a lot of Berlin and Berlin, thought a lot of Whiting. That was in 1905.

I dreamed of working with Whiting one day, but never dreamed it would happen -- and later, to become part of a guy who had been part of another guy, if you know what I mean? Oh my goodness, we were playing one day, "Belive it, Beloved" and Irving Berlin was there listening to it. He liked it a lot. He was singing it, singing it right out, and suddenly George says, "Come on, let's get out of here, if he can sing it, he can rewrite it!"
Well, that was in the vaudeville days.

I made about seven trips to New York City in February, March and April of 1979, to interview JC. A few times, we'd begin our interviews on tape, but he had increasing difficulty in breathing, and requested that we stop.
"Let's do it next time" he'd say. He was getting progressively worse and I was progressively concerned. This is one of the tapes in which he reluctantly participated:
.. and it's so lovely being here with you.
